narration.text: In summer, this field leans toward the Sun.
Sunlight strikes it steeply, and the oak tree stands in full leaf.
In autumn, the field leans neither toward the Sun nor away from it.
Daylight lasts about half the day, and the oak tree turns golden.
In winter, the same field leans away from the Sun.
Sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin, and the bare oak tree stands in snow.
The tilt, not the distance from the Sun, makes these seasons.
In spring, the same oak tree buds again.

brief.title: Tilt, not distance, makes the seasons
brief.summary: Why summer and winter come from the tilt of the ground toward or away from the Sun, not from the distance to it, shown by one oak tree through a year.
